text_original: UNESCO describes buurisame, served to children during Fichee-Chambalaalla, as a meal prepared from false banana, milk and butter.
text_en: Among the Sidama, buurisame, the festival dish served during Fichee-Chambalaalla, is made from false banana (enset), milk and butter.

source.title: Fichee-Chambalaalla, New Year festival of the Sidama people
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: FAO reports that Ethiopia's first Food-Based Dietary Guidelines were published in 2022, led and coordinated by the Ethiopian Public Health Institute and endorsed by the Ministries of Health, Agriculture and Education.
text_en: Ethiopia published its first food-based dietary guidelines in 2022, led by the Ethiopian Public Health Institute and endorsed by the health, agriculture and education ministries.

source.title: Food-based dietary guidelines - Ethiopia
source.publisher: FAO - Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

text_original: According to FAO, the Ethiopian dietary guidelines' visual food guide is a meskel flower, which signals the start of the new year and harvest season, with six food groups in its petals (cereals, grains, roots and tubers; legumes; nuts and oilseeds; animal-source foods; fruits and vegetables; fats and oils) and a glass of water at the centre.
text_en: Ethiopia's food guide is drawn as a meskel flower, a symbol of the new year and harvest, with six food groups in the petals and a glass of water in the middle.

source.title: Food-based dietary guidelines - Ethiopia
source.publisher: FAO - Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

text_original: FAO states that the diet modelling for the Ethiopian guidelines was done for non-fasting, continuous fasting and intermittent fasting diets at three energy levels (1250, 2300 and 2700 kcal per day).
text_en: Ethiopia's dietary guidelines were modelled separately for non-fasting, continuous-fasting and intermittent-fasting diets at 1,250, 2,300 and 2,700 kcal/day.

source.title: Food-based dietary guidelines - Ethiopia
source.publisher: FAO - Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

text_original: The FAO page lists 11 key messages of the Ethiopian dietary guidelines, including eating at least 4 food groups per meal and 6 per day, 80-120 g of legumes daily, limiting salt to under 5 g a day, and limiting alcoholic drinks, factory-processed and homemade, to no more than 2 glasses per week.
text_en: Ethiopia's 2022 dietary guidelines advise at least 4 food groups per meal (6 daily), 80-120 g of legumes a day, under 5 g of salt daily and no more than 2 alcoholic drinks a week.

source.title: Food-based dietary guidelines - Ethiopia
source.publisher: FAO - Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

text_original: A 2019 review in Annals of Botany (AGRIS record) states that enset currently provides the staple food for approximately 20 million Ethiopians and has only ever been domesticated in the Ethiopian Highlands, where smallholder farmers cultivate hundreds of landraces.
text_en: A 2019 review reports enset is a staple for about 20 million Ethiopians, domesticated only in the Ethiopian Highlands, where smallholders grow hundreds of landraces.

source.title: Enset in Ethiopia: a poorly characterized but resilient starch staple
source.publisher: FAO AGRIS record of Annals of Botany 123(5), 2019 (Oxford University Press)

text_original: According to the same review, enset can be harvested at any time of year over several years, is somewhat drought-tolerant, and provides starch as well as fibres, medicines, animal fodder, roofing and packaging, with significant cultural importance.
text_en: Enset can be harvested year-round over several years and yields food starch, fibre, medicine, fodder, roofing and packaging, and carries cultural importance.

source.title: Enset in Ethiopia: a poorly characterized but resilient starch staple
source.publisher: FAO AGRIS record of Annals of Botany 123(5), 2019 (Oxford University Press)

text_original: A 2022 review by University of Gondar authors describes injera as a thin, soft, fermented baked bread made from cereal flour fermented for 24 to 96 hours, using teff, sorghum, maize, wheat or barley, with teff injera preferred by many Ethiopians.
text_en: Injera is a fermented flatbread made from cereal flour (teff, sorghum, maize, wheat or barley) fermented 24-96 hours; a 2022 review says many Ethiopians prefer teff injera.

source.title: A Review on Factors Influencing the Fermentation Process of Teff (Eragrostis teff) and Other Cereal-Based Ethiopian Injera
source.publisher: International Journal of Food Science (2022), University of Gondar authors, via PubMed Central

text_original: The review describes mixing teff flour and water in a bohaka (clay, metal or wood container) with irsho/ersho from the previous batch, then boiling about 10% of the fermented paste with three parts water (absit) and adding it back for a second fermentation of 1.5 to 2 hours; a portion of the yellowish liquid is kept for the next batch.
text_en: Traditional injera batter is fermented in a bohaka with starter from the previous batch; about 10% of the paste is boiled with three parts water (absit) and added back for 1.5-2 more hours.

source.title: A Review on Factors Influencing the Fermentation Process of Teff (Eragrostis teff) and Other Cereal-Based Ethiopian Injera
source.publisher: International Journal of Food Science (2022), University of Gondar authors, via PubMed Central

text_original: According to the review, injera made without absit tends to be powdery with fewer of the 'eyes' (bubbles) that Ethiopian consumers prize, and the number of large eyes on the upper surface determines its attractiveness.
text_en: A 2022 review says injera without absit is powdery and has fewer of the prized 'eyes' (bubbles), which determine how attractive it is.

source.title: A Review on Factors Influencing the Fermentation Process of Teff (Eragrostis teff) and Other Cereal-Based Ethiopian Injera
source.publisher: International Journal of Food Science (2022), University of Gondar authors, via PubMed Central

text_original: The review distinguishes aflegna, a thick, sweet injera baked after 12-24 hours of fermentation, from traditional injera fermented 48-72 hours and komtata, made from over-fermented batter; baking on the mitad takes 2-3 minutes.
text_en: Aflegna is a thick sweet injera from a 12-24 hour batter, traditional injera ferments 48-72 hours, komtata comes from over-fermented batter, and each injera bakes in 2-3 minutes on the mitad.

source.title: A Review on Factors Influencing the Fermentation Process of Teff (Eragrostis teff) and Other Cereal-Based Ethiopian Injera
source.publisher: International Journal of Food Science (2022), University of Gondar authors, via PubMed Central

text_original: The review lists injera, kocho, awaze, tella, tej and borde among Ethiopia's traditional fermented foods and drinks, describing kocho as a lactic-acid fermented food of southern Ethiopia made from enset pseudostem, pulverized corm and decorticated pulp.
text_en: Ethiopian traditional fermented foods include injera, kocho, awaze, tella, tej and borde; kocho is a lactic-fermented enset food of southern Ethiopia.

source.title: A Review on Factors Influencing the Fermentation Process of Teff (Eragrostis teff) and Other Cereal-Based Ethiopian Injera
source.publisher: International Journal of Food Science (2022), University of Gondar authors, via PubMed Central

text_original: The 2024-25 EDHS reports that 16.2% of children aged 6-23 months were fed at least five of eight defined food groups the previous day (minimum dietary diversity), 34.3% were given a sweet beverage and 18.2% were fed unhealthy foods.
text_en: In 2024-25, only 16.2% of Ethiopian children aged 6-23 months met minimum dietary diversity; 34.3% had a sweet beverage and 18.2% unhealthy foods the previous day.

source.title: Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey 2024-25: Key Indicators Report
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) and ICF

text_original: In Platt's ethnographic study of Ethiopian women, the buna coffee ceremony has three rounds of boiling: Abol (the first, strongest), Hulettengana (second, made by adding water to the same grounds, weaker) and Baraka (third, 'the last one'), whose root brk relates to blessing.
text_en: In the buna coffee ceremony described by Platt (2013), coffee is served in three rounds - Abol, Hulettengana and Baraka - with later rounds made from the same grounds and Baraka linked to the word for blessing.

source.title: Sisters in Transition: Moving from the Buna Coffee Ritual to Relief Society (in: By Our Rites of Worship, 2013)
source.publisher: Religious Studies Center, Brigham Young University (J. B. Platt)

text_original: According to the study, a snack is served with buna to extend the gathering, typically roasted barley (kolo) or popcorn, varying with the hostess's means; the coffee is prepared in a jebena, with incense and grass used in the ritual space.
text_en: In the buna ceremony, roasted barley (kolo) or popcorn is typically served, depending on the hostess's means, and the jebena, incense and grass are part of the set-up.

source.title: Sisters in Transition: Moving from the Buna Coffee Ritual to Relief Society (in: By Our Rites of Worship, 2013)
source.publisher: Religious Studies Center, Brigham Young University (J. B. Platt)

text_original: Study participants said a buna tray often holds twelve cups regardless of how many women gather, that the absence of incense negates a proper ceremony, and that the hostess sits low near the stove, which they linked to humility.
text_en: Women in Platt's study said a proper buna uses twelve cups on the tray and incense, with the hostess sitting low by the stove.

source.title: Sisters in Transition: Moving from the Buna Coffee Ritual to Relief Society (in: By Our Rites of Worship, 2013)
source.publisher: Religious Studies Center, Brigham Young University (J. B. Platt)

text_original: EveryCulture's Ethiopia entry describes injera, a spongy unleavened teff bread, as the staple of every meal, eaten by hand: pieces are torn off and used to scoop stews (wat) of vegetables such as carrots, cabbage, spinach, potatoes and lentils, with berbere (a red-pepper-based spice) the most common seasoning.
text_en: According to the EveryCulture entry, meals are built around teff injera eaten by hand with stews (wat) of vegetables and lentils seasoned with berbere.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: The entry says most people observe Old Testament food taboos as prescribed by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, avoiding animals with uncloven hooves or that do not chew the cud, so pork is nearly impossible to obtain, and that animals must be slaughtered with the head turned east and the throat cut in the name of the Trinity (Christian slaughterer) or of Allah (Muslim slaughterer).
text_en: EveryCulture reports that Orthodox-observant dietary rules exclude pork, and that animals are slaughtered facing east with an invocation of the Trinity (Christians) or Allah (Muslims).

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: According to the entry, during Christian fasting periods no animal products may be eaten and no food or drink consumed from midnight until 3 p.m. on weekdays, while on Saturdays and Sundays animal products are avoided but there is no time restriction.
text_en: In the EveryCulture description of Christian fasting, weekday fasts bar animal products and all food or drink from midnight to 3 p.m.; on Saturday and Sunday only animal products are avoided.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: EveryCulture describes tej as a honey wine reserved for special occasions, made of honey and water flavoured with gesho twigs and leaves and traditionally drunk from tube-shaped flasks.
text_en: Tej is described as an occasion drink of honey and water flavoured with gesho and traditionally served in tube-shaped flasks.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: The entry lists dining etiquette: wash hands before a meal, eat from a communal dish by hand, the guest initiates eating, pull injera only from the space directly in front of you, replace depleted portions quickly, and take part in conversation since giving full attention to the meal is impolite.
text_en: In this account, meals are eaten from a communal dish after hand-washing, guests start first, each person pulls injera from the area in front of them, and talking during the meal is polite.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: In the 2020/21 Meher season, private peasant holdings in Ethiopia used 48.60% of their teff production for household consumption, 34.79% for sale and 12.94% for seed.
text_en: In 2020/21 Ethiopian smallholders consumed 48.6% of their teff harvest at home, sold 34.8% and kept 12.9% as seed.

source.title: Agricultural Sample Survey 2020/21 (2013 E.C.), Vol. VII: Report on Crop and Livestock Product Utilization (Private Peasant Holdings, Meher Season)
source.publisher: Central Statistical Agency (now Ethiopian Statistical Service)

text_original: According to the 2020/21 survey, the share of teff kept for household consumption was 67.43% in Tigray (17.51% sold), 54.57% in Amhara (30.01% sold), 50.11% in Oromia (32.20% sold) and 44.60% in North Shewa zone of Amhara (39.32% sold).
text_en: In 2020/21 the share of teff eaten at home was 67.4% in Tigray, 54.6% in Amhara, 50.1% in Oromia and 44.6% in North Shewa, where 39.3% was sold.

source.title: Agricultural Sample Survey 2020/21 (2013 E.C.), Vol. VII: Report on Crop and Livestock Product Utilization (Private Peasant Holdings, Meher Season)
source.publisher: Central Statistical Agency (now Ethiopian Statistical Service)

text_original: The survey report describes enset as a staple food of southern and western Ethiopia and records that 75.78% of enset production was used for household consumption and 16.72% sold in 2020/21.
text_en: The 2020/21 survey calls enset a staple of southern and western Ethiopia and records 75.8% consumed at home and 16.7% sold.

source.title: Agricultural Sample Survey 2020/21 (2013 E.C.), Vol. VII: Report on Crop and Livestock Product Utilization (Private Peasant Holdings, Meher Season)
source.publisher: Central Statistical Agency (now Ethiopian Statistical Service)

text_original: The 2020/21 survey found that 63.37% of cereals produced by private peasant holdings were used for household consumption (maize 72.07%, finger millet 71.99%, sorghum 70.43%), and concluded that peasant farmers consume most of what they produce, leaving little to sell.
text_en: In 2020/21, smallholders ate 63.4% of the cereals they grew (maize 72.1%, finger millet 72.0%, sorghum 70.4%).

source.title: Agricultural Sample Survey 2020/21 (2013 E.C.), Vol. VII: Report on Crop and Livestock Product Utilization (Private Peasant Holdings, Meher Season)
source.publisher: Central Statistical Agency (now Ethiopian Statistical Service)

text_original: FIFA's member-association profile lists the Ethiopian Football Federation as a member of the Confederation of African Football (CAF), based at Addis Ababa Stadium, with separate national coaches for the men's and women's teams (profile accessed 2026-09-29).
text_en: As of FIFA's profile accessed 29 September 2026, the Ethiopian Football Federation belongs to CAF, is based at Addis Ababa Stadium and has separate national coaches for its men's and women's teams.

source.title: Ethiopian Football Federation - Organisation
source.publisher: FIFA (Inside FIFA member association profile)

text_original: Capital Ethiopia reports that the Great Ethiopian Run, a 10 km mass-participation race, was started in 2001 by double Olympic champion Haile Gebrselassie, with Meskel Square as its start and finish, and that Gebrselassie and Berhane Adere won the first edition; the race is nicknamed 'Haile's Run' (YeHaile Rucha).
text_en: The Great Ethiopian Run 10 km in Addis Ababa was founded in 2001 by Haile Gebrselassie, starts and finishes at Meskel Square, and is nicknamed 'YeHaile Rucha' (Haile's Run).

source.title: 23 Years of Mass-Participation Running in Ethiopia (opinion article)
source.publisher: Capital Ethiopia (Capital Newspaper)

text_original: According to Capital Ethiopia (2023), the Great Ethiopian Run is Africa's biggest mass-participation road race; participants run, jog, walk and dance the 10 km course, and the event is described as closer to a street carnival than a running competition, with more than 40,000 finishers expected in 2023.
text_en: The Great Ethiopian Run is described as more street carnival than race: tens of thousands (over 40,000 expected in 2023) run, jog, walk and dance 10 km in Addis Ababa.

source.title: 23 Years of Mass-Participation Running in Ethiopia (opinion article)
source.publisher: Capital Ethiopia (Capital Newspaper)

text_original: Capital Ethiopia reports that places in the Great Ethiopian Run typically go on sale during the rainy season and sell out in under a week, and that the Ministry of Tourism and Ethiopian Airlines are closely involved in the event.
text_en: Great Ethiopian Run places usually go on sale in the rainy season and sell out within a week, with the Ministry of Tourism and Ethiopian Airlines closely involved.

source.title: 23 Years of Mass-Participation Running in Ethiopia (opinion article)
source.publisher: Capital Ethiopia (Capital Newspaper)

text_original: The article notes that children's races on the Saturday before the main race involve around 3,000 children and often carry public-health messages, such as 'Together, We End Polio' and 'For Every Child: Vaccines' in 2023.
text_en: Around 3,000 children take part in Saturday children's races alongside the Great Ethiopian Run, which in 2023 carried polio and vaccination messages.

source.title: 23 Years of Mass-Participation Running in Ethiopia (opinion article)
source.publisher: Capital Ethiopia (Capital Newspaper)

text_original: Capital Ethiopia states that the elite fields typically come from Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Eritrea, that the elite 10 km races have always been won by Ethiopian athletes, and that the race has served as a springboard for young Ethiopian athletes such as Tsegaye Kebede and Netsanet Gudeta.
text_en: Elite fields in the Great Ethiopian Run come from Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Eritrea; Ethiopians have won every elite race, and the event has launched young runners' careers.

source.title: 23 Years of Mass-Participation Running in Ethiopia (opinion article)
source.publisher: Capital Ethiopia (Capital Newspaper)

text_original: CAF's member-association page lists the Ethiopian Football Federation as created in 1943, affiliated to FIFA in 1952 and to CAF in 1957.
text_en: According to CAF, the Ethiopian Football Federation was created in 1943, joined FIFA in 1952 and joined CAF in 1957.

source.title: Ethiopian Football Federation - Ethiopia (CAF member association page)
source.publisher: Confederation of African Football (CAF)

text_original: CAF's page places the Ethiopian Football Federation in the CECAFA regional grouping, based at Addis Ababa Stadium, and lists separate coaches for the men's and women's national teams (page accessed 2026-09-29).
text_en: CAF lists Ethiopia's football federation within CECAFA, based at Addis Ababa Stadium, with separate men's and women's national coaches (as of 29 September 2026).

source.title: Ethiopian Football Federation - Ethiopia (CAF member association page)
source.publisher: Confederation of African Football (CAF)

text_original: A 2003 questionnaire study of 114 members of Ethiopia's national athletics team and 111 controls found marathon athletes were over-represented as coming from the regions of Arsi and Shewa (73% of marathoners, 43% of 5-10 km athletes, 29% of other track and field athletes, versus 15% of controls).
text_en: A 2003 survey of Ethiopia's national athletics team found 73% of marathon runners came from Arsi and Shewa versus 15% of controls (43% for 5-10 km, 29% for other track and field).

source.title: Demographic characteristics of elite Ethiopian endurance runners (Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise 35(10), 2003)
source.publisher: University of Brighton research repository (Scott et al.)

text_original: The same study reports that languages of Cushitic origin predominated among marathon athletes (75%), 5-10 km athletes (52%) and other track and field athletes (46%), versus 30% of controls.
text_en: Cushitic languages were spoken by 75% of national-team marathoners, 52% of 5-10 km runners and 46% of other track and field athletes, versus 30% of controls (2003 study).

source.title: Demographic characteristics of elite Ethiopian endurance runners (Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise 35(10), 2003)
source.publisher: University of Brighton research repository (Scott et al.)

text_original: The study found that 68% of marathon athletes, 31% of 5-10 km athletes and 16% of other track and field athletes had run to school, compared with 24% of controls, and that endurance athletes generally traveled farther to school.
text_en: In the 2003 study, 68% of national-team marathoners had run to school (24% of controls), and endurance athletes typically traveled farther to school.

source.title: Demographic characteristics of elite Ethiopian endurance runners (Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise 35(10), 2003)
source.publisher: University of Brighton research repository (Scott et al.)

text_original: A 2021 peer-reviewed study of cultural sport in two Dawro woredas (Tercha and Tocha), based on 10 sport professionals, 8 elders and 12 young people, found that Dawro cultural sports are practised by most of Dawro society and contribute to health, fitness and social interaction.
text_en: A 2021 study in Tercha and Tocha woredas found Dawro cultural sports are widely practised and contribute to fitness, health and social interaction.

source.title: The Progress and Identification of Cultural Sport of Dawuro and Their Contribution to Social Interaction and Fitness (abstract page)
source.publisher: International Journal of Sports Science and Physical Education (Science Publishing Group), Jimma University authors

text_original: The same study reports that Dawro cultural sports are now dominated by modern sports, are not included in all Dawro games and are at the edge of disappearing, and it recommends that elders, sport experts and youth cooperate to pass the sports to young people through training places and inter-woreda competitions.
text_en: The Dawro study finds cultural sports are being displaced by modern sports and risk disappearing, recommending elder-youth transmission and inter-woreda competitions.

source.title: The Progress and Identification of Cultural Sport of Dawuro and Their Contribution to Social Interaction and Fitness (abstract page)
source.publisher: International Journal of Sports Science and Physical Education (Science Publishing Group), Jimma University authors

text_original: The Ethiopian Postal Service's 1984 stamp text describes gebeta as a pit-and-pebble board game played in hollows scooped in the ground or carved in rock, or on a long wooden board, said to have been a favourite pastime of Ethiopians in the sixth century; it is played at wedding ceremonies, at harvest time and, in the south, after circumcision rites, mostly by elderly men and children and rarely by women.
text_en: According to Ethiopost's 1984 stamp text, gebeta is a pit-and-pebble game played on ground hollows, rock or wooden boards at weddings, harvest time and (in the south) after circumcision rites, chiefly by elderly men and children.

source.title: Ethiopian Traditional Sport (stamp issue of 7 December 1984, stamp introduction text)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Postal Service (Ethiopost)

text_original: According to the same text, genna, a game resembling cricket or hockey, is played by various Ethiopian nationalities regardless of religion; before Menilik's dynasty it was played by northern groups such as the Amhara, Tigrai and Agaw and later became popular in the south, and it is played by elderly men and women as well as children.
text_en: Ethiopost describes genna (a hockey-like stick game) as played across nationalities and religions, first by northern groups such as Amhara, Tigrai and Agaw, later also in the south, by men, women and children.

source.title: Ethiopian Traditional Sport (stamp issue of 7 December 1984, stamp introduction text)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Postal Service (Ethiopost)

text_original: The stamp text says a genna match starts with the players encircling the field, two captains meeting at the centre where the ball is buried and touching sticks three times; teams may come from different villages or from one village, and the genna stick is made of bent tree branches hardened by fire.
text_en: In genna, players encircle the field, two captains touch sticks three times over the buried ball, teams may be village against village, and sticks are fire-hardened bent branches (Ethiopost, 1984).

source.title: Ethiopian Traditional Sport (stamp issue of 7 December 1984, stamp introduction text)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Postal Service (Ethiopost)

text_original: Ethiopost describes Feres Gugs as a game exclusive to Ethiopia that demands skilled horsemanship on tough ponies, the word 'gugs' referring to a fast rider able to protect himself from and injure an enemy.
text_en: Ethiopost's 1984 stamp text presents Feres Gugs as an Ethiopian horsemanship game requiring skilled riding, with 'gugs' denoting a fast rider.

source.title: Ethiopian Traditional Sport (stamp issue of 7 December 1984, stamp introduction text)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Postal Service (Ethiopost)

text_original: According to the text, in the countryside tigil (wrestling) pairs young males by age and strength, often village against village; bouts are held near a village after the harvest and stocking of grain but before threshing, on soft grass or hay, and the first to fall loses points until combatants are forced to retire through exhaustion.
text_en: Ethiopost says tigil wrestling in the countryside matches youths by age and strength, often between villages, on grass or hay after harvest and before threshing, with points lost by falling.

source.title: Ethiopian Traditional Sport (stamp issue of 7 December 1984, stamp introduction text)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Postal Service (Ethiopost)

text_original: EBR reports (2018-19) that the head of the Ethiopian Cultural Sports Federation, Belayneh Haile, said there are more than 290 cultural games in the country, and that the federation had extended its standardised list from six to nine and then 11 games and was working to reach 13.
text_en: Ethiopia's Cultural Sports Federation head said in 2018-19 that over 290 cultural games exist, and the federation's standardised list had grown from six to nine to 11 games.

source.title: Ethiopia's Neglected Sports (Ethiopian Business Review, issue no. 69, Dec 2018-Jan 2019)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Business Review (EBR)

text_original: The federation organises three annual competitions and festivals attracting close to 1,000 delegates competing in 11 cultural games, takes part in inter-regional schools' sport competitions, and cultural sports also appear at women's championships (EBR, 2018-19).
text_en: According to EBR, the Cultural Sports Federation runs three annual events with about 1,000 delegates in 11 games and joins inter-regional school competitions and women's championships.

source.title: Ethiopia's Neglected Sports (Ethiopian Business Review, issue no. 69, Dec 2018-Jan 2019)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Business Review (EBR)

text_original: EBR notes that Emperor Tewodros II recruited the best wrestlers (gibgib/tigil) from across the country to contest foreigners, that Emperor Menilik II and Empress Taytu organised their own 'ye gena chewata' (hockey) teams to face each other on special occasions, and that Taytu used gebeta to draw customers to the hotel that bore her name.
text_en: Ethiopian Business Review recounts that Tewodros II recruited wrestlers for contests with foreigners, Menilik II and Empress Taytu fielded gena teams, and Taytu used gebeta to attract hotel guests.

source.title: Ethiopia's Neglected Sports (Ethiopian Business Review, issue no. 69, Dec 2018-Jan 2019)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Business Review (EBR)

text_original: The federation head told EBR that public interest in cultural games is low, that the media approach the federation about once a year for 'ye gena chewata' around Christmas, and that the federation's budget from the Ministry of Youth and Sport was ETB 410,000 a year, covering only two training sessions a year.
text_en: In EBR's 2018-19 report, the federation described low public interest in cultural games, yearly media attention around Christmas gena matches, and an ETB 410,000 annual state budget.

source.title: Ethiopia's Neglected Sports (Ethiopian Business Review, issue no. 69, Dec 2018-Jan 2019)
source.publisher: Ethiopian Business Review (EBR)

text_original: UNESCO states that Sidama parents transmit the Fichee-Chambalaalla tradition to their children orally and through participation in the celebration, and that women in particular pass knowledge and skills of hairdressing and preparing buurisame to their daughters and other girls in their villages.
text_en: In Sidama communities, parents pass the Fichee tradition to children orally and through participation, and women teach hairdressing and buurisame preparation to daughters and other village girls.

source.title: Fichee-Chambalaalla, New Year festival of the Sidama people
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: In the Oromo Gada system as described by UNESCO, class membership is open to men whose fathers are already members, while women are consulted for decision-making on protecting women's rights.
text_en: In the Oromo Gada system, membership of a Gada class passes through fathers to sons, and women are consulted on decisions concerning the protection of women's rights.

source.title: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: The 2016 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey reports an average household size of 4.6 members, one-quarter of households headed by women, and nearly half (47%) of the population under age 15.
text_en: According to the 2016 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (CSA and ICF), the average household size was 4.6 members, about one quarter of households were headed by women, and 47% of the population was under age 15.

source.title: 2016 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey Key Findings
source.publisher: Central Statistical Agency (Ethiopia) and ICF, published via The DHS Program

text_original: In the 2016 EDHS the median age at first marriage was 17.1 years for women and 23.7 years for men aged 25-49; 58% of women were married by age 18 compared with 9% of men.
text_en: In the 2016 EDHS, women aged 25-49 had a median age at first marriage of 17.1 years and men 23.7 years; 58% of women and 9% of men were married by age 18.

source.title: 2016 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey Key Findings
source.publisher: Central Statistical Agency (Ethiopia) and ICF, published via The DHS Program

text_original: The 2016 EDHS found that women with no education marry at a median age of 16.3 years, 7.7 years earlier than women with more than secondary education (24.0 years).
text_en: In the 2016 EDHS, women with no education married at a median age of 16.3 years versus 24.0 years for women with more than secondary education.

source.title: 2016 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey Key Findings
source.publisher: Central Statistical Agency (Ethiopia) and ICF, published via The DHS Program

text_original: In the 2016 EDHS, 11% of women aged 15-49 and 5% of men aged 15-49 were in a polygynous union.
text_en: According to the 2016 EDHS, 11% of women and 5% of men aged 15-49 were in polygynous unions.

text_en: In Wolaita Gifaataa celebrations, girls help mothers with food, drink and house decoration, boys help fathers with firewood, bonfires and home repairs, and elders resolve conflicts and give farming advice and blessings.

text_en: Xeer Ciise, the oral customary law of Somali-Issa communities, has a political constitution, a penal code centred on reconciliation and compensation and a social conduct code that includes respecting women's and children's rights.

text_en: In 2024/25, 27.3% of recent internal migrants moved to join or live with family and 10.2% for marriage.

text_en: According to the 2024-25 EDHS, among people aged 15-49, 61% of women and 52% of men were in a union, 29.5% of women and 46.0% of men had never married, and 9% of women versus 2% of men were divorced, separated or widowed.

text_en: Ethiopia's total fertility rate was 4.0 in 2024-25 (4.5 rural, 3.2 urban); urban fertility rose from 2.3 in the 2016 survey to 3.2.

source.title: Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey 2024-25: Key Indicators Report
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) and ICF

text_en: In 2024-25, 35% of married women used contraception (injectables 20%, implants 10%, pills 2%) and 15% had unmet need.

source.title: Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey 2024-25: Key Indicators Report
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) and ICF

text_en: In 2024-25, 61.4% of births were in a health facility - 89.4% urban vs 49.4% rural - from 97.9% in Addis Ababa to 34.2% in Somali and 33.3% in Afar.

source.title: Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey 2024-25: Key Indicators Report
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) and ICF

text_en: In 2024-25, 72.5% of Ethiopian babies were breastfed within an hour of birth and 57.3% of infants under six months were exclusively breastfed.

source.title: Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey 2024-25: Key Indicators Report
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) and ICF

text_original: Platt reports that children of about three or four are sent to call women to buna ('Buna! Buna! Buna!'), that girls learn by observation rather than lessons, and that the typical age to first prepare buna was around ten, first for the family; hosting one's own buna typically came with marriage or having one's own home.
text_en: In Platt's study, small children call women to buna, girls learn by observing and first prepare it around age ten for the family, and hosting one's own buna typically follows marriage or setting up a home.

source.title: Sisters in Transition: Moving from the Buna Coffee Ritual to Relief Society (in: By Our Rites of Worship, 2013)
source.publisher: Religious Studies Center, Brigham Young University (J. B. Platt)

text_original: The study reports that when a family member dies, women close to the mourning relatives gather and may stay for several weeks, consoling through the buna ceremony while preparing meals and doing household tasks.
text_en: In Platt's study, when someone dies, close women friends of the bereaved may stay for weeks, holding buna, cooking and doing household work.

source.title: Sisters in Transition: Moving from the Buna Coffee Ritual to Relief Society (in: By Our Rites of Worship, 2013)
source.publisher: Religious Studies Center, Brigham Young University (J. B. Platt)

text_original: According to the entry, arranged marriages were the norm though becoming less common, especially in cities; elders travel from the groom's home to the bride's parents to ask for the marriage and traditionally decide when and where the ceremony is held, and both families brew drinks and prepare much food, especially meat dishes.
text_en: EveryCulture reports that marriage proposals traditionally involve elders visiting the bride's parents, elders set the ceremony's time and place, and both families prepare food and drink.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: The entry says a dowry from the groom's family to the bride's family is common, varying with wealth and possibly including livestock or money, and that in the takelil wedding, held in Orthodox churches, the couple agree never to divorce, a commitment that has become rare.
text_en: In this account, a dowry from the groom's side (livestock, money) is common, and the Orthodox takelil wedding includes a vow never to divorce but has become rare.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: EveryCulture states that the household is traditionally larger than a Western nuclear unit, headed by the oldest male; children are expected to care for parents so three to four generations may live together, though urban living is changing this and urban residents feel responsible for sending money to rural relatives.
text_en: The entry describes multigenerational households headed by the eldest male, with children expected to support parents, and urban migrants remitting money to rural families.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: The entry says descent is traced through both parents but the male line is more valued, villages are often made up of kin groups that support one another, and elders or groups of elders settle disputes within a kin group or clan.
text_en: EveryCulture reports that descent is reckoned on both sides but favours the male line, and elders settle disputes within kin groups or clans.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: EveryCulture describes the iddir as an association of neighbours, workmates, friends or kin whose members pay a set monthly contribution to provide financial help in times of illness, death, fire or theft; it became prevalent with urban society and iddirs have also funded schools and roads.
text_en: The iddir is described as a burial-and-emergency mutual-aid association in which members contribute monthly to help families during illness, death or property loss.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: UNESCO states that Gada classes are taught by oral historians covering history, laws, rituals, time reckoning, cosmology, myths, rules of conduct and the function of the Gada system, and that knowledge about Gada is transmitted to children in the home and at school.
text_en: Among the Oromo, oral historians teach Gada classes about history, laws, rituals, time reckoning, cosmology, myths, rules of conduct and how Gada works, and children learn about Gada at home and at school.

source.title: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO states that Xeer Ciise is transmitted informally through tales, proverbs, games, poetry and initiation rites, and also through formal educational curricula, panel discussions, symposiums and print and electronic media.
text_en: Somali-Issa communities pass on Xeer Ciise through tales, proverbs, games, poetry and initiation rites as well as school curricula, panel discussions and media.

source.title: Xeer Ciise: Oral customary laws of Somali-Issa communities in Ethiopia, Djibouti and Somalia
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: The Ministry of Education's Education Statistics Annual Abstract for 2022/23 describes the system as six primary grades (Grades 1-6, ages 7-12) and two middle grades (Grades 7-8, ages 13-14), followed by secondary Grades 9-12; data for that edition exclude Tigray because teaching-learning had not restarted there.
text_en: In 2022/23 Ethiopia's general education comprised primary Grades 1-6 (ages 7-12), middle Grades 7-8 (ages 13-14) and secondary Grades 9-12; Tigray was not covered by that year's statistics.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: According to the 2022/23 abstract, Ethiopian pre-primary education is delivered in four modalities: three-year Kindergarten (mostly run by NGOs, communities, private and faith-based bodies), one-year Child to Child, a one-year 'O' Class reception year at government primary schools for 6-year-olds, and a 2-3 month Accelerated School Readiness programme.
text_en: Pre-primary education in Ethiopia (2022/23) runs through Kindergarten (3 years, mostly non-government), Child to Child (1 year), the 'O' Class (1 year, for 6-year-olds in government primary schools) and a 2-3 month Accelerated School Readiness programme.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The Ministry of Education abstract explains that in the Child to Child modality older children (Grade 5 or above) play with younger siblings and neighbourhood children aged 4-6, supervised by qualified teachers, to learn counting, colours and letters before primary school.
text_en: In Ethiopia's Child to Child pre-school modality, older children from Grade 5 up play with younger siblings and neighbours aged 4-6 under teacher supervision to teach counting, colours and letters.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The 2022/23 abstract reports a national pre-primary gross enrolment ratio of 50.0%, with regional GERs from 9.0% in Somali and 23.4% in Afar to 101.3% in Harari and 137.5% in Addis Ababa.
text_en: In 2022/23 Ethiopia's pre-primary GER was 50.0% nationally, ranging from 9.0% in Somali and 23.4% in Afar to 101.3% in Harari and 137.5% in Addis Ababa.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: In 2022/23 the 'O' Class had a national GER of 85.8% and made up the majority of pre-primary enrolment; SNNP had the highest GER at 149.6%, while Somali (24.3%) and Addis Ababa (5.9%) were lowest.
text_en: The 'O' Class reception year accounted for most pre-primary enrolment in 2022/23 (GER 85.8%), highest in SNNP (149.6%) and lowest in Addis Ababa (5.9%) and Somali (24.3%).

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The 2022/23 abstract gives a gross enrolment ratio of 96.1% and a net enrolment ratio of 83.3% for Grades 1-8; GER ranged from 57.8% in Afar to 160.5% in Gambella.
text_en: In 2022/23 Ethiopia's Grades 1-8 GER was 96.1% and NER 83.3%, with regional GERs from 57.8% in Afar to 160.5% in Gambella.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: In 2022/23 the primary (Grades 1-6) GER was 105.4% while the middle level (Grades 7-8) GER was 65.9%, which the Ministry reads as low transition between the two levels.
text_en: The 2022/23 GER dropped from 105.4% in Grades 1-6 to 65.9% in Grades 7-8, indicating many pupils do not transition to middle school.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The abstract reports 2021/22 dropout rates of 16% in primary and 15% in middle school, with Grade 1 the highest at 21%; Afar had the highest primary dropout rate (20.5%).
text_en: In 2021/22 Ethiopia's dropout rate was 16% in primary and 15% in middle school, highest in Grade 1 (21%), and highest in Afar for primary (20.5%).

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: According to the 2022/23 abstract, the survival rate to Grade 7 was 39% for girls and 34% for boys, and the Grade 8 completion rate was 61.0% in 2022/23 compared with 46.7% in 2013/14.
text_en: In 2022/23 the survival rate to Grade 7 was 39% (girls) and 34% (boys), and the Grade 8 completion rate reached 61.0%, up from 46.7% in 2013/14.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The Ministry of Education abstract records that Ethiopia's School Feeding Program began in 1994 as a pilot in 40 schools in Tigray, Amhara, Afar and Oromia, and that in 2022/23 6.9 million pre-primary and primary children received school meals.
text_en: Ethiopia's school feeding began in 1994 with a 40-school pilot in Tigray, Amhara, Afar and Oromia; in 2022/23 it reached 6.9 million pre-primary and primary pupils.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The abstract states that the number of pupils receiving school meals almost tripled compared with the previous year because an extensive school feeding programme began in Oromia region in 2022, reaching over 5 million children.
text_en: School meal coverage nearly tripled in 2022/23 mainly because Oromia started a large programme in 2022 that reached over 5 million children.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

subregion: Afar; Somali; Benishangul-Gumuz; Gambela; pastoralist woredas of Oromia, SNNP and SWEP
text_original: The Ministry of Education abstract says the government gives special support to the emerging regions (Afar, Somali, Benishangul-Gumuz and Gambela) and to 63 pastoralist woredas (45 in Oromia, 7 in SNNP and 11 in South West Ethiopia), where pastoralist livelihoods involve moving from place to place with a strong reliance on livestock; pastoralist areas made up 8.2% of Grades 1-8 enrolment in the three latter regions in 2022/23.
text_en: Ethiopia's 2022/23 education abstract identifies 63 pastoralist woredas (45 Oromia, 7 SNNP, 11 South West Ethiopia) plus four emerging regions as needing special support because pastoralist life involves movement and livestock reliance.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: Among responding primary and middle schools in 2022/23, 27.7% had electricity, 39.2% had a functional library and 36.2% had a functional water supply.
text_en: In 2022/23 among responding primary and middle schools, 27.7% had electricity, 39.2% a functional library and 36.2% functional water supply.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The 2022/23 abstract reports a national pupil-teacher ratio of 36.4 for Grades 1-8 (standard: 50), from 19.7 in Addis Ababa to 75.7 in Somali.
text_en: In 2022/23 Ethiopia's pupil-teacher ratio for Grades 1-8 was 36.4 against a standard of 50, ranging from 19.7 in Addis Ababa to 75.7 in Somali.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: In 2022/23 Ethiopia had 37,051 primary and middle schools (Grades 1-8), 91.7% government-owned, with 15,167 in Oromia; Addis Ababa was the exception, having more non-government than government primary schools.
text_en: Ethiopia had 37,051 Grades 1-8 schools in 2022/23, 91.7% government-owned and 15,167 in Oromia; only Addis Ababa had more non-government than government primary schools.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The abstract explains that schools in woredas are usually grouped into clusters of five or more to share resources, and reports 7,047 cluster schools in 2022/23, 2,862 of them in Oromia.
text_en: Ethiopian schools are typically grouped into clusters of five or more per woreda to share facilities; in 2022/23 there were 7,047 clusters, 2,862 in Oromia.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_original: The abstract states that the revised Education and Training Policy of 2023 provides two years of free and compulsory education for 5- and 6-year-old children, with pre-primary for 4-year-olds optional, though some regions offer a full three-year pre-primary.
text_en: Under Ethiopia's revised 2023 Education and Training Policy, two years of pre-primary are free and compulsory for ages 5 and 6, age 4 is optional, and some regions already run three years.

source.title: Education Statistics Annual Abstract (ESAA) 2022/23 (2015 E.C.)
source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education, Ethiopia - EMIS and ICT Executive Office

text_en: In 2024-25, 32.5% of women and 16.7% of men aged 15-49 had no schooling; 9.2% of women and 12.7% of men had attended beyond secondary.

source.title: Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey 2024-25: Key Indicators Report
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) and ICF

text_en: Among 15-19-year-old women in 2024-25, ever-pregnant rates fell from 24.3% for those with no education to 5.5% (secondary) and 0.2% (beyond secondary); overall 10.2%.

source.title: Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey 2024-25: Key Indicators Report
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) and ICF

text_en: According to EveryCulture, around 1999 university education was free, with entry decided by a national exam that admitted about 20% of test-takers and department quotas.

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_en: EveryCulture reports that urban children start school around age five if fees are affordable, while in rural areas few schools and farm work limited attendance (c. 2001).

source.title: Ethiopia (Countries and Their Cultures entry, by Adam Mohr)
source.publisher: EveryCulture / Countries and Their Cultures (Advameg; Gale reference encyclopedia)

text_original: According to Sidama oral tradition as recorded by UNESCO, Fichee commemorates a Sidama woman who visited her parents and relatives once a year after her marriage, bringing buurisame, a meal of false banana, milk and butter, which she shared with neighbours; Fichee has since become a unifying symbol of the Sidama people.
text_en: Among the Sidama, the New Year festival Fichee-Chambalaalla commemorates, in oral tradition, a married woman's yearly visit to her relatives with buurisame (false banana, milk and butter) shared with neighbours, and serves as a unifying symbol of the Sidama people.

source.title: Fichee-Chambalaalla, New Year festival of the Sidama people
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO records that each year Sidama astrologers determine the correct date for Fichee-Chambalaalla, and the date is then announced to the clans.
text_en: Among the Sidama, the date of Fichee-Chambalaalla is set each year by astrologers and announced to the clans, so the festival is moveable.

source.title: Fichee-Chambalaalla, New Year festival of the Sidama people
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: On the first day of Fichee-Chambalaalla, Sidama children go from house to house to greet their neighbours, who serve them buurisame; every member of the community takes part in the traditional songs and dances irrespective of age, gender and social status.
text_en: On the first day of the Sidama New Year festival, children visit neighbours' houses to greet them and are served buurisame; songs and dances involve every community member regardless of age, gender or social status.

source.title: Fichee-Chambalaalla, New Year festival of the Sidama people
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: During Fichee-Chambalaalla, Sidama clan leaders advise the people to work hard, respect and support the elders, and abstain from cutting down indigenous trees, begging, indolence, false testimony and theft.
text_en: During the Sidama New Year festival, clan leaders give moral advice: work hard, respect and support elders, and avoid cutting indigenous trees, begging, idleness, false testimony and theft.

source.title: Fichee-Chambalaalla, New Year festival of the Sidama people
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: According to UNESCO, Gada meetings and ceremonies take place under a sycamore tree, considered the symbol of Gada, and major Oromo clans have established Gada centres and ceremonial spaces according to territory.
text_en: Gada meetings and ceremonies among the Oromo are held under a sycamore tree, the Gada symbol, and major clans maintain territorial Gada centres and ceremonial spaces.

source.title: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO records that the Ethiopian Epiphany commemoration starts on the eve of the main festival, on 18 January, known as Ketera; on that eve people escort their parish church tabot (replica of the Ark of the Covenant), carried by a priest, to Timkete-Bahir (a pool, river or artificial reservoir) with a great ceremony.
text_en: On 18 January, the eve called Ketera, Ethiopian Epiphany participants escort their parish church's tabot, carried by a priest, in ceremony to the Timkete-Bahir water site.

source.title: Ethiopian epiphany
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: According to UNESCO, people spend the night of the Epiphany eve attending night-long prayers and hymn services including the Eucharistic Liturgy.
text_en: During Ethiopian Epiphany, worshippers spend the eve night at night-long prayers and hymn services, including the Eucharistic Liturgy.

source.title: Ethiopian epiphany
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO states that hundreds of thousands participate in the Epiphany festival on 19 January, which starts early with pre-sunrise rituals followed by the sprinkling of blessed water on the congregation; at around 10 a.m. each tabot begins its procession back to its church with traditional and religious songs.
text_en: On 19 January, Ethiopian Epiphany begins with pre-sunrise rituals and sprinkling of blessed water; around 10 a.m. each tabot returns to its church in a procession with religious and traditional songs.

source.title: Ethiopian epiphany
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO says the viability of Ethiopian Epiphany is ensured through continued practice, with Orthodox clergy pivotal: they sing the praises for the rituals and hymns, carry the Ark, and preach relevant texts.
text_en: Orthodox clergy play a pivotal role in Ethiopian Epiphany by singing the hymns, carrying the Ark (tabot) and preaching.

source.title: Ethiopian epiphany
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO's documentation describes youth singers from church Sunday schools leading the Epiphany procession with the begena (ten-string harp) and traditional songs, performing hymns composed by St. Yared, and youth blowing the meleket (Ethiopian trumpet) before the Arks.
text_en: In Ethiopian Epiphany processions, Sunday-school youth sing St. Yared's hymns, accompanied by the begena harp, and blow the meleket trumpet before the tabots.

source.title: Ethiopian epiphany
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO's Epiphany page notes that on an island in Lake Zeway the parish tabot is accompanied with boats, that in Axum priests perform the rhythm 'Worede World Emsemayat Wuste Mitmakat', and that where a large pool exists, as at Fasiledes' bath in Gondar, celebrants may immerse themselves in the water.
text_en: Local Epiphany variations documented by UNESCO include boat-accompanied tabots on a Lake Zeway island, a priestly rhythm performed in Axum, and immersion in the pool at Fasiledes' bath in Gondar.

source.title: Ethiopian epiphany
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO states that Ethiopian Epiphany is an occasion when traditional dances and songs of the nations and nationalities of Ethiopia are performed, promoting cultural exchange and traditional dress and ornamental styles.
text_en: Ethiopian Epiphany doubles as an occasion for performances of traditional dances and songs of Ethiopia's different nations and nationalities and for displaying traditional dress.

source.title: Ethiopian epiphany
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO reports that Maskel is celebrated on 26 September to commemorate the unearthing of the True Holy Cross, beginning with construction of the Damera bonfire in Maskel Square in Addis Ababa, a conical pyre decorated with green grass and Abyssinian daisies symbolizing the New Year; the patriarch of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church lights it.
text_en: Maskel (26 September) starts with building the Damera pyre in Maskel Square, Addis Ababa, decorated with grass and Abyssinian daisies symbolising the New Year; the Orthodox patriarch lights it at the climax.

source.title: Commemoration feast of the finding of the True Holy Cross of Christ
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO notes that Maskel is a time when families get together and migrant workers return home, reunions that bring an inflow of money, information and new ideas from urban centres to rural areas, and that personal quarrels must be resolved before the celebration.
text_en: Around Maskel, families reunite and migrant workers return home, bringing money, information and ideas from towns to rural areas; disputes are settled before the celebration.

source.title: Commemoration feast of the finding of the True Holy Cross of Christ
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO records that Gifaataa is a New Year festival celebrated by the Wolaita community between mid-September and early October; before it starts people clean their surroundings and return home to be with their families, and disputes are resolved peacefully in preparation for the new year.
text_en: Among the Wolaita, before Gifaataa (mid-September to early October) people clean their surroundings, return to their families and settle disputes peacefully.

source.title: Gifaataa (New Year festival of the Wolaita community)
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: According to UNESCO, on the main day of Gifaataa Wolaita families share raw meat and local beer and receive blessings from elders; in the evenings the community gathers around a bonfire for rituals, singing and dancing, and the ten-day festival ends with a large celebration called 'goolo-igetta' with horse riding, music and final blessings.
text_en: In Gifaataa, Wolaita families share raw meat and local beer and receive elders' blessings; evenings feature bonfire rituals, songs and dances, and the ten days end with 'goolo-igetta', including horse riding.

source.title: Gifaataa (New Year festival of the Wolaita community)
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: UNESCO describes Shuwalid as an annual three-day festival of the Harari people that marks the end of six days of fasting to compensate omissions during Ramadan, celebrated at the shrines of Aw Shulum Ahmed and Aw Akebara at the main entrance gates of the walled city of Harar.
text_en: Shuwalid is a three-day Harari festival ending six days of fasting made up after Ramadan, held at the shrines of Aw Shulum Ahmed and Aw Akebara at Harar's walled-city gates.

source.title: Shuwalid festival
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_original: According to UNESCO, Shuwalid begins with supplications and spiritual songs, followed by scripture reading, music and dance, and ends with words of blessing; elders share knowledge and give blessings to the next generations while youth learn cultural values, norms and traditions.
text_en: The Harari Shuwalid festival moves from supplications and spiritual songs to scripture reading, music, dance and blessings, and lets elders pass on knowledge and youth learn values.

source.title: Shuwalid festival
source.publisher: UNESCO - Intangible Cultural Heritage (Representative List)

text_en: The 2024-25 EDHS sample of women aged 15-49 was 43.1% Orthodox, 29.1% Muslim, 25.4% Protestant, 0.9% Catholic and 0.4% traditional; men were 41.7% Orthodox, 30.3% Muslim and 26.1% Protestant.

text_original: Platt reports that rural Ethiopian women in the study gathered for buna at least once a day, typically at midday, that women in Addis Ababa gathered daily though less consistently, and that a spontaneous ceremony may be held when visitors arrive; the ceremony takes about an hour.
text_en: In Platt's study, buna gatherings were at least daily and usually midday in rural areas, daily but less consistent in Addis Ababa, and could be improvised for visitors.

text_original: The study describes buna as a women's gathering where participants talk freely, which they called a 'time to be free', and notes that the ceremony also accompanies funerals and marriages.
text_en: Participants in Platt's study described buna as a women's space for open conversation ('a time to be free'), also held around funerals and marriages.

text_original: EveryCulture lists Ethiopia's major state holidays as New Year's Day (11 September), the Victory of Adwa (2 March), Patriots' Victory Day (6 April), Labour Day (1 May) and the Downfall of the Derg (28 May), and notes that most celebrations are religious, including Christmas on 7 January, Epiphany on 19 January, Easter and Meskel.
text_en: The EveryCulture entry names Ethiopian state holidays (New Year 11 Sept, Adwa 2 March, Patriots' Victory 6 April, Labour Day 1 May, Derg downfall 28 May) and notes most festivals are religious (Christmas 7 Jan, Epiphany 19 Jan, Easter, Meskel).

text_en: EveryCulture reports that Christians and Muslims sometimes visit one another's places of worship to seek health or prosperity.

text_en: Eskesta is described as a shoulder-movement dance accompanied by the kabaro drum and the one-string masinqo fiddle.

text_original: The 2024/25 National Integrated Household Survey Labour Force Module estimates 54.3 million people in Ethiopia's labour force among the 80.1 million aged 10 and above, a labour force participation rate of 67.8% (64.7% in February 2021); Gambella (52.8%) and Dire Dawa (56.5%) had the lowest regional rates.
text_en: In the ESS 2024/25 survey the labour force participation rate for people aged 10+ was 67.8% (54.3 million people), up from 64.7% in 2021, with the lowest regional rates in Gambella (52.8%) and Dire Dawa (56.5%).

text_original: The survey reports a national employment-to-population ratio of 61.3% in 2024/25 (59.5% in 2021, excluding Tigray), highest in South West Ethiopia (73.5%) and Amhara (70.3%) and lowest in Dire Dawa (48.3%) and Gambella (49.4%).
text_en: Ethiopia's 2024/25 employment-to-population ratio was 61.3%, from 73.5% in South West Ethiopia and 70.3% in Amhara down to 48.3% in Dire Dawa and 49.4% in Gambella.

source.title: Key Findings Report on Labour Market Indicators - National Integrated Household Survey (2024/25), Labour Force Module

text_original: According to the 2024/25 NIHS, 63.3% of employed persons work as skilled agricultural and fishery workers, 18.5% in elementary occupations and 0.4% as managers; the report notes agriculture's occupational share grew from 38% to 63.3% over past decades.
text_en: In 2024/25, 63.3% of Ethiopia's employed people were skilled agricultural and fishery workers, 18.5% worked in elementary occupations and 0.4% were managers.

source.title: Key Findings Report on Labour Market Indicators - National Integrated Household Survey (2024/25), Labour Force Module
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS)

text_original: The 2024/25 NIHS reports that agriculture provides 69.4% of employment, services 23.9% and industry 6.7%; agriculture accounts for 81.7% of rural employment while services account for 61.7% of urban employment.
text_en: In 2024/25 agriculture employed 69.4% of Ethiopian workers (81.7% in rural areas), services 23.9% (61.7% in urban areas) and industry 6.7%.

source.title: Key Findings Report on Labour Market Indicators - National Integrated Household Survey (2024/25), Labour Force Module
source.publisher: Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS)

text_original: In 2024/25, 62.5% of employed persons in Ethiopia were self-employed, 22.9% were employees (including paid apprentices and interns) and 13.6% were unpaid family workers.
text_en: In 2024/25 Ethiopia's employed were 62.5% self-employed, 22.9% employees and 13.6% unpaid family workers.

text_en: In 2024/25 Ethiopian paid employees earned on average Birr 6,704 per month: Birr 7,534 for men, Birr 5,473 for women (27.4% gap), Birr 7,484 urban and Birr 4,626 rural.

text_original: Among people outside the labour force in 2024/25, homemaking was the reason for 43.3% of women versus 5.1% of men, while being in study accounted for 56.2% of men versus 32.3% of women.
text_en: In the 2024/25 ESS survey, 43.3% of economically inactive women were homemakers (5.1% of men), and 56.2% of inactive men were students (32.3% of women).

text_en: ESS 2024/25: unemployment was 9.6% (5,238,234 people) - 12.8% for women, 7.2% for men, 17.2% urban and 7.4% rural.

text_en: ESS 2024/25: youth (15-35) unemployment was 12.9% - 20.6% urban, 10.2% rural, 17.4% women, 9.1% men - and 20.3% in Addis Ababa.

text_en: In the ESS 2024/25 migration report, 36.1% of recent internal migrants moved to search for work (41.2% urban, 29.9% rural).

text_en: ESS 2024/25 estimates 847,664 emigrants, 547,353 of them women (426,099 rural women), and 95.2% emigrated to search for work.

text_original: EveryCulture describes the debo as the most widespread rural social welfare association: a farmer having difficulty tending his fields invites neighbours to work on a set day, provides food and drink for that day and later contributes labour when others in the debo need help; it is also used for housing construction.
text_en: A farmer can call a debo, inviting neighbours to help on a set day in return for food and drink and reciprocal labour, and debos are also used for building houses.

text_original: The entry says that traditionally men plow, harvest, trade, slaughter animals, herd, build houses and cut wood, while women are in charge of cooking, brewing beer, cutting hops, buying and selling spices, making butter and collecting wood and water; it adds that the division is less pronounced in cities.
text_en: EveryCulture describes a traditional rural division of labour - men plowing, harvesting, herding and building; women cooking, brewing, butter-making and fetching wood and water - less pronounced in urban areas.

text_en: EveryCulture reports that metalworking, leatherworking and pottery are among occupations regarded as low status and sometimes socially isolated.
